steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting bGPT, a byte-level model trained with next byte prediction to process binary data and simulate the digital world. Contrast it with language models, explain why bytes matter, describe the model's advantages and outline the experiments.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Deep learning on human-interpretable media; language models
2. The overlooked native binary data and why bytes matter
3. Introducing bGPT and its two advantages
4. Experiments and significance

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Media and LMs
- deep learning focused on media easy for humans to interpret: text, audio, images; relevant to human communication/understanding
- text central to conveying human intelligence -> Language Models (LMs)
- LM principle: tokenize text, predict next token -> comprehend human language and intelligence
- recent: tokenization extended to modalities beyond text -> more holistic understanding of real world, emulate human intelligence

2. Bytes
- models mostly operate on media data; overlook omnipresent native binary data
- bytes = foundation of all digital data, devices, software; from computer processors to operating systems in everyday electronics
- next byte prediction -> possible paradigm shift; truly understand and simulate all activities in digital world
- benefits in conventional and underexplored areas: cybersecurity, computer diagnostics, data compression, reverse-engineering source code from binary

3. bGPT
- binary data processing + digital world modelling via next byte prediction
- digital world: media files + digital systems, from hardware architectures to complex algorithms
- directly interprets and manipulates binary data -> intrinsic, holistic understanding
- 1) Interpreting Digital System: learns patterns of digital systems from byte sequences; predict, simulate, diagnose algorithm or hardware behaviour; reconstruct complex systems from binary data
- 2) Unified Modelling: various data types in one framework, everything a byte sequence; simpler modelling, easy integration of data sources

4. Experiments
- 1) well-studied: generative modelling and classification on digital media (text, audio, images)
- 2) underexplored, binary-native: data conversion (algorithm simulation), CPU state modelling (hardware simulation)
- significance: step towards holistic, unified deep learning; new perspective on modelling the digital world

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning research has focused on digital media files that humans can easily interpret, like text, audio and images, because they are directly relevant to how humans communicate and understand things. Text especially plays a central role in conveying human intelligence, and it has led to Language Models (LMs). The basic principle of LMs is to tokenize text and predict the next token in a sequence, and this lets them comprehend human language and intelligence. Recent work also extends tokenization to other modalities beyond text, so that LMs can get a more holistic understanding of the real world and emulate human intelligence.

But these deep learning models mostly work with media data, and they overlook the native binary data that is everywhere in the digital world. Bytes are the foundation of all digital data, devices and software, from computer processors to the operating systems in everyday electronics. So training models to predict the next byte could lead to a paradigm shift in deep learning, because it would let them really understand and simulate all the activities in the digital world. This is useful in conventional areas but also in areas that are not explored much, like boosting cybersecurity, improving computer diagnostics, optimizing data compression, and even complex tasks like reverse-engineering the source code of software from its binary representation.

3. bGPT
- binary data processing + digital world modelling via next byte prediction
- digital world: media files + digital systems, from hardware architectures to complex algorithms
- directly interprets and manipulates binary data -> intrinsic, holistic understanding
- 1) Interpreting Digital System: learns patterns of digital systems from byte sequences; predict, simulate, diagnose algorithm or hardware behaviour; reconstruct complex systems from binary data
- 2) Unified Modelling: various data types in one framework, everything a byte sequence; simpler modelling, easy integration of data sources

4. Experiments
- 1) well-studied: generative modelling and classification on digital media (text, audio, images)
- 2) underexplored, binary-native: data conversion (algorithm simulation), CPU state modelling (hardware simulation)
- significance: step towards holistic, unified deep learning; new perspective on modelling the digital world

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning research has focused on digital media files that humans can easily interpret, like text, audio and images, because they are directly relevant to how humans communicate and understand things. Text especially plays a central role in conveying human intelligence, and it has led to Language Models (LMs). The basic principle of LMs is to tokenize text and predict the next token in a sequence, and this lets them comprehend human language and intelligence. Recent work also extends tokenization to other modalities beyond text, so that LMs can get a more holistic understanding of the real world and emulate human intelligence.

But these deep learning models mostly work with media data, and they overlook the native binary data that is everywhere in the digital world. Bytes are the foundation of all digital data, devices and software, from computer processors to the operating systems in everyday electronics. So training models to predict the next byte could lead to a paradigm shift in deep learning, because it would let them really understand and simulate all the activities in the digital world. This is useful in conventional areas but also in areas that are not explored much, like boosting cybersecurity, improving computer diagnostics, optimizing data compression, and even complex tasks like reverse-engineering the source code of software from its binary representation.

In this paper we introduce bGPT, which is a model for binary data processing and digital world modelling using next byte prediction. The digital world is not only the digital media files that deep learning models traditionally focus on, it also includes the complicated realm of digital systems, from hardware architectures to complex algorithms. bGPT goes beyond traditional deep learning boundaries because it interprets and manipulates binary data directly, which gives a more intrinsic and holistic understanding of the digital world. It has two advantages. 1) Interpreting Digital System: bGPT is trained on byte sequences, so it can learn the patterns of digital systems, and this lets it predict, simulate and diagnose the behaviour of algorithms or hardware. With this, complex systems can be reconstructed from binary data. 2) Unified Modelling: bGPT puts various data types into a single framework by treating everything as a byte sequence. This makes modelling simpler and makes it easy to integrate different data sources.

Our experiments cover two main areas: 1) tasks that are well-studied, like generative modelling and classification on digital media data (e.g., text, audio, and images); and 2) tasks that are relatively underexplored and intrinsic to binary-native operations, including data conversion and CPU state modelling, which stand for algorithm simulation and hardware simulation. Studying byte models is a significant step towards deep learning that is holistic and unified, and it also gives a new perspective on modelling the digital world.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning research has focused on digital media files that are easily interpretable by humans, such as text, audio, and images [1,2,3], because of their direct relevance to human communication and understanding. Text in particular plays a central role in conveying human intelligence and has led to the emergence of Language Models (LMs) [4,5,6,7,8,9]. The fundamental principle of LMs is to tokenize text [10,11,12,13] and predict the next token in a sequence, which enables them to comprehend human language and intelligence. Recent advancements further extend tokenization to modalities beyond text [14,15], allowing LMs to attain a more holistic understanding of the real world and to emulate human intelligence [16,17,18,19].

However, these deep learning models predominantly operate on media data, overlooking the native binary data that is omnipresent in the digital world. Bytes are the foundation of all digital data, devices, and software, from computer processors to the operating systems of everyday electronics. Training models for next byte prediction can therefore potentially lead to a paradigm shift in deep learning, allowing them to truly understand and simulate all activities in the digital world. This has practical benefits not only in conventional areas but also in underexplored ones, such as boosting cybersecurity [20], improving computer diagnostics [21], optimizing data compression [22], and even complex tasks like reverse-engineering the source code of software from its binary representation.

In this paper, we introduce bGPT, a model designed for binary data processing and digital world modelling by next byte prediction. The digital world includes not only digital media files, the traditional focus of deep learning models, but also the intricate realm of digital systems, ranging from hardware architectures to complex algorithms. bGPT goes beyond traditional deep learning boundaries by directly interpreting and manipulating binary data, enabling a more intrinsic and holistic understanding of the digital world. Its advantages are two-fold: 1) Interpreting Digital System: by training on byte sequences, bGPT can learn the patterns of digital systems, which enables it to predict, simulate, and diagnose algorithm or hardware behaviour, and allows complex systems to be reconstructed from binary data. 2) Unified Modelling: bGPT integrates various data types into a single framework by treating everything as a byte sequence, which simplifies modelling and allows easy integration of various data sources.

Our experiments cover two main areas: 1) well-studied tasks such as generative modelling and classification on digital media data (e.g., text, audio, and images); and 2) relatively underexplored tasks intrinsic to binary-native operations, including data conversion and CPU state modelling, which represent algorithm and hardware simulation, respectively. The study of byte models marks a significant step towards holistic and unified deep learning, and also offers a new perspective on modelling the digital world.
